meta.description: Not Rockefeller. Quote Investigator traces it to an 1893 Rothschild anecdote; the Rockefeller credit first appears in a 1990 quotation collection.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The way to make money is to buy when blood is running in the streets'?
meta.ogDescription: An 1893 Rothschild anecdote, compacted into a proverb by 1942, and pinned on John D. Rockefeller only in 1990. No primary source exists.

answer.label: Not John D. Rockefeller — a Rothschild anecdote hardened into a proverb
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · ancestor anecdote in print from 1893 · credited to Rockefeller only from 1990
answer.sourceLine: Rockefeller never wrote or said this, in any documented source. Quote Investigator traces the saying to an anecdote in The Globe of Toronto on 29 December 1893, in which an unnamed Rothschild tells a nervous French investor that “if the streets were not running with blood you couldn’t buy rentes at present prices” — and QI considers that anecdote apocryphal ↗. The compact wording circulated for decades as a Rothschild dictum: in 1964 Harry D. Schultz printed “Buy when the blood is running in the streets” and credited Rothschild. Rockefeller’s name was attached only in 1990, in a Robert Byrne quotation collection, with no source given.
answer.confidenceText: The Rockefeller credit is documented no earlier than a 1990 quotation anthology, which supplies no source; the near-identical wording was in print as a Rothschild saying in 1964, and nothing resembling the saying appears anywhere in Rockefeller’s own 1909 memoir.

source.excerpt: A French investor at a critical time was advised by one of the Rothschilds to buy rentes. “What!” he cried. “Buy Government securities while the streets of the capital are running with blood?” “My friend,” was the reply, “if the streets were not running with blood you couldn’t buy rentes at present prices.”
trail: 1893 — an anecdote, not a quotation. Quote Investigator’s earliest match is The Globe of Toronto, 29 December 1893, in which an unnamed Rothschild tells a French investor that “if the streets were not running with blood you couldn’t buy rentes at present prices” ↗. QI considers the anecdote apocryphal, noting how long after the events it implies it first surfaces.

1942–1964 — the anecdote becomes a rule. The Springfield Daily Republican of 19 December 1942 refers to “the Rothschild investment dictum to ‘buy when the streets run with blood’,” and Harry D. Schultz’s Bear Markets (Prentice-Hall, 1964) prints at page 164: “Rothschild once advised, ‘Buy when the blood is running in the streets.’” ↗ The wording is essentially the modern one — and the name on it is Rothschild.

1990 — Rockefeller’s name appears. Robert Byrne’s The Fourth — And by Far the Most Recent 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (Atheneum, 1990) gives quotation 301 as “The way to make money is to buy when blood is running in the streets. John D. Rockefeller (1839–1937)” ↗ — the earliest Rockefeller credit QI documents, and the only citation Wikiquote offers for it ↗.

Rockefeller’s own book says nothing like it. A full-text search of his memoir Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909) ↗ returns no passage resembling the saying: “blood” occurs there only in his account of Dr. Alexis Carrel’s blood-transfusion operation (pp. 151–152) and in the phrase “cold-blooded,” and “street” only in his boyhood job hunt, a Cleveland address and a passage about street beggars. His one documented buy-the-panic statement is a different sentence entirely: the New York Herald Tribune of 31 October 1929 reported that he and his son “had been heavy buyers of stocks for investment in the last few days, and would continue to buy at present prices” ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the ancestor of the proverb, not the proverb, and not Rockefeller. It is the earliest match Quote Investigator finds, transcribed from The Globe of Toronto for 29 December 1893: an anecdote with an unnamed Rothschild and no maxim in it. The compact one-line dictum was distilled out of stories like this over the following half-century.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for this wording, because no author for it has ever been identified. The documented carriers point in both directions: the 1893 Globe anecdote it descends from is long out of copyright in the United States, while the two books that carry the modern wording — Harry D. Schultz’s Bear Markets (Prentice-Hall, 1964) and Robert Byrne’s anthology (Atheneum, 1990) — are themselves in copyright as compilations, and neither claims to have coined it.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.kicker: The man who gets the credit
author.heading: So why does Rockefeller’s name stick to it?
author.metaLine: 1839–1937 · American oil industrialist & philanthropist; founder of Standard Oil
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller (8 July 1839 – 23 May 1937) founded the Standard Oil Company in 1870 and became the dominant figure of the American petroleum industry before turning to large-scale philanthropy. He was an operator and owner, not a market speculator — his fortune came from refining, pipelines and consolidation, and his own memoir, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), is a book about building businesses rather than trading panics. He did, though, make one famous buy-the-panic statement: during the October 1929 crash he announced that he and his son had been purchasing sound common stocks. That single real episode is the nearest thing in his life to the sentiment of this proverb — and a plausible reason a Rothschild saying drifted onto his name.

misattribution.heading: Six claimants, no evidence
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb wearing a succession of borrowed names. The wording has been stable for decades; the credit line has changed roughly once a decade, which is the clearest sign that nobody can point to an original.

items.why: The earliest Rockefeller credit Quote Investigator documents is quotation 301 in Robert Byrne’s 1990 anthology, which prints the line and the dates “(1839–1937)” and nothing else ↗. Wikiquote reproduces the line under Rockefeller but cites only that same Byrne entry, adding that it is “attributed elsewhere to Nathan M. Rothschild” ↗. No speech, letter, interview or book of Rockefeller’s has ever been produced for it.

QI finds the Rothschild in the earliest (1893) telling is unnamed; the New York Times of 21 January 1894 first names “old Baron Rothschild,” a 1916 market letter says Anselm, a 1973 Boston Sunday Globe item says Lionel, and the 1987 book Blood in the Streets credits Nathan M. Rothschild in its epigraph ↗. QI treats the underlying anecdote as apocryphal and identifies no specific Rothschild as its source.
A 1980 syndicated column credited the saying to the financier Bernard Baruch ↗ — another name for the same sentence, with no more support than the others.

The habit persists in mainstream coverage: Forbes opens a contrarian-investing explainer with “Baron Rothschild … is credited with saying that ‘the time to buy is when there’s blood in the streets’” ↗, and supplies no citation for either that or the “even if the blood is your own” extension.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who coined it. What is documented is an 1893 newspaper anecdote about an unnamed Rothschild, a compact “Rothschild investment dictum” in circulation by 1942, and a run of later, mutually incompatible credits — Rockefeller’s among them, and one of the last to arrive ↗.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: Investing proverbs need a rich ancestor, and the Rothschilds were the richest name available. What Quote Investigator actually finds in 1893 is not a maxim at all but a scene: a French investor recoils at buying government rentes while the streets of the capital run with blood, and an unnamed Rothschild points out that the blood is precisely why the bonds are cheap. It is a story with a punchline, not a slogan. The 1893 telling names neither the Rothschild nor the city; the Paris Commune of 1871 setting arrives only with the 1894 retellings, and that later-added specificity is part of why QI treats the story as apocryphal.

The slogan was manufactured later, by compression. By 19 December 1942 the Springfield Daily Republican could refer in passing to “the Rothschild investment dictum to ‘buy when the streets run with blood’” — the anecdote had become a rule ↗. From there the credit line became a free variable: an unnamed Rothschild, then “old Baron Rothschild,” then Anselm, then Lionel, then Nathan, then Bernard Baruch, then Rockefeller. The sentence stayed put while the author rotated, which is the signature of a proverb rather than a quotation.
context.detailsSummary: The attestation ladder, as Quote Investigator documents it
detailsBody: 1893–1916 — the anecdote years. QI’s earliest match is The Globe of Toronto, 29 December 1893, where the Rothschild is unnamed; the New York Times of 21 January 1894 is the first to specify “old Baron Rothschild,” and a 1916 market letter by Thomas Gibson credits “Anselm Rothschild” ↗. QI also notes the gap between the events the anecdote implies (the Paris Commune, 1871) and its first appearance in print, which is one reason it treats the story as apocryphal.

1942–1964 — the proverb years. The Springfield Daily Republican of 19 December 1942 already treats it as a standing “Rothschild investment dictum,” and in 1964 Harry D. Schultz’s Bear Markets: How to Survive and Make Money in Them prints it at page 164 in almost exactly its modern form: “Rothschild once advised, ‘Buy when the blood is running in the streets.’ He said it all.” ↗

1973–1994 — the credit roulette. A 1973 Boston Sunday Globe item names Lionel Rothschild; a 1980 syndicated column hands it to Bernard Baruch; the 1987 book Blood in the Streets uses it as an epigraph credited to Nathan M. Rothschild; Byrne’s 1990 anthology credits John D. Rockefeller; and on 28 October 1994 the Chicago Tribune quotes Mark Mobius with the extended form, “you must buy when blood is running on the streets — even when it’s your own” ↗.
context.pull: The saying was in print as a Rothschild dictum in 1964. Rockefeller’s name was bolted on in 1990.
